Patient demographics:
  age: 77
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Surgeon
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Tactile (Temperature): A specific temperature on the skin, Stress: Stress, Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Positive Feelings: push away positive emotions because they feel unsafe, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events
  Threat: Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm, Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
  Memory: Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

Vignette:
Thirty-four years ago, during a prolonged emergency laparotomy, an electrical fault ignited the surgical drapes. Vinh stood at the foot of the operating table, watching the flames climb the sterile field while the attending physician scrambled to douse the fire. He witnessed the attending suffer third-degree burns on his forearm, the sharp crackle of burning synthetic material, and the suffocating acrid smoke that coated the back of his throat. The specific searing heat that brushed his own cheek as he stepped forward to help left a lasting thermal imprint. He remained in the theatre that day, but the event lodged in his nervous system, and his body began to react as though he were still standing in that room. Within weeks, he started feeling jumpy. His shoulders tightened at the unexpected crash of a dropped tray or the sudden ring of a telephone. He was certain that disaster could strike without warning, that the room could ignite again at any moment, and he had to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next. The memories never lined up in a clear line; one afternoon he would feel the raw, crushing panic of the event with such force that his hands shook, yet he could not picture the drapes or the physician’s face. The distress felt detached, as though it belonged to a man whose name he could no longer recall, while his own body kept responding to a threat that had long since passed. He recognized that something was wrong with him as a person, that a surgeon who could not steady his own hands in a crisis was unfit for the field. To cope, he tried hard not to think about the theatre, forcing his attention to chart reviews and morning rounds. He pushed away positive emotions whenever they surfaced, telling himself that joy was a luxury that felt dangerously unsafe. He avoided television programmes and films, unable to bear scenes involving fire, emergencies, or even dramatic tension. Over the following months, these habits calcified. He stopped attending his grandchildren’s recitals because the unpredictable noise of crowds felt like a threat to his equilibrium. At home, he flinched when the oven timer clicked, and he refused to let his wife hold his hand while they watched the evening news. His steady avoidance of media and positive feelings coexisted with a quiet distance between him and his spouse; she learned to speak in careful tones, and their shared table grew heavy with unspoken things. He took on more rounds than his body could sustain, sometimes forgetting to take his blood pressure medication or driving his car with less caution than he would have once allowed, all while stress accumulated as his schedule tightened. Even as he transitioned to a part-time consulting role, the demands of the hospital kept the pressure high. In the prep room, the faint tang of burnt cauterized tissue would rise from the surgical suites above, and he would immediately step back, his pulse jumping as the specific heat of the sterilization autoclave’s steam seemed to press against his gloves. He felt that his body kept reacting as if he were still in danger even when he was safe, and the constant vigilance sapped his ability to rest. Now seventy-seven, Vinh finally sat in a clinic chair after his wife placed a referral on his kitchen counter. He could not pinpoint a single breaking point, only the accumulation of days where he kept pushing himself past exhaustion. He was most afraid of losing the last remnants of his career and his ability to care for his wife, yet he hoped someone might help him untangle the heat and the smoke from his present life. He wanted to stop feeling like his own nervous system was an adversary, and to let himself sit at his daughter’s dinner table without bracing for the next sudden noise.
